paragraphs.text: III. THE LIFE OF THE MOST BLESSED MAN EPIPHANIUS, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF TICINUM.

An uncertain necessity presses me to take up this work. The task set before me is neither free of labour for me nor safe from the wrangling of detractors. A twofold caution governs its style: on one side it expects richness of talent, and on the other the tongue must rein in its wealth of narration. When someone is too eager to exalt with windy praise those persons whom vain conceit in this world thinks most eminent, or through poverty of eloquence keeps them within the bare limits of their deeds, either course is judged ungrateful in their eyes. In praises it is shameful to forge things that even the person described would not recognize. In the same way it is thought injurious, and a cause for grief, to pass over in silence what a true account could raise high. For the good deeds of our forebears take their worth among us from the skill of the one who tells them. What a vein poor in words has undertaken to set forth either perishes from memory or passes to posterity diminished. And praise more licentious than is just plucks away as much glory as it adds falsehood. Indeed it often happens that a heap of praise without credibility diminishes the good deeds of many. A narrative that swells with lies is empty, while one that does not go through to the end is untimely and far too beggarly. Therefore, as I set out to tell the life of the most blessed Epiphanius, bishop of Ticinum, I call on the Holy Spirit as witness and companion of his deeds. With the Spirit's help I hope to hand down to pages that will live through the ages the glory of that most serene conscience which the Spirit granted him, so that his fame, which will offer an example of virtues, may never die. The narrowness of my eloquence, which must run under fixed rules, may so hem me in that I can do no more than set out in order the bare facts of his merits. Even so, I shall find nothing among his labours so ordinary or lowly that I must puff it up with the bubbles of lively speech, as most writers do. I will also call as witnesses affairs that are still warm, and I will display his trophies, still smoking and adorned with the spoils of the despoiled devil. No one recounts things that are almost before people's eyes and all too well known unless he is confident of the truth. So, to the very people I would avoid if I meant to tell fictions, as one aware of his own impudence, I am reading back what their own eyes have seen.

The distinguished man Epiphanius, then, was by origin a native of the town of Ticinum. He was begotten by his father Maurus and born of his mother Focaria, who was also related to the line of the holy confessor and bishop Mirocles. They were people descended from a clear spring of free and noble birth. But why should I rehearse the privileges of blood of those whose son is himself the head of their family and nobility? Under his predecessor, the most upright Bishop Crispinus, he began his apprenticeship in the heavenly army. At about eight years old he took up the office of lector in the church, after a sign had first been shown from heaven. For while he was still among the rattles of nursing infancy, a great many people saw his cradle shine with light from above. A radiance lit him up and went before him, revealing the future brightness of his mind and marking even then, with a prefiguring light, the splendour that would follow in his character. He soon mastered the abbreviations of shorthand and the various signs that compress a multitude of words. Enrolled among the stenographers, he shone, and already began to take down dictation as one who could himself dictate without reproach from good men. As time and labour went on, and divine favour brought him to his sixteenth year, he was already pondering grey-haired counsels in his boyhood. Modesty, the mother of good works, flourished in him above all else. He served the bishop so gladly that if any task was done by someone else, he took it hard that the service had been stolen from him. He received the old with gravity and the young with courtesy, and even then he boldly restrained wrongdoers. He was submissive to his superiors and obedient to his elders when they enjoined holy things. He was gentle and obliging to his equals, and shared himself with those below him in pure charity. He set himself above no one, though by his religious course along the heavenly path he went ahead of all. He was free of the love of praise, though things worthy of praise grew in him daily. And though he accomplished deeds worthy of glory from hour to hour, he thought their fruit and reward would perish if people made public what he showed in secret to God alone. In short, mindful of the apostle's saying, he rejected flattery and applauded himself inwardly, with his conscience as witness, in recognition of good work.

I will not refuse to touch on this as well: his beauty, a bodily light, was an index of his soul. The grace of his form shone out so strongly against his own wishes that it could not be overthrown, though so strong a man fought against it. His cheeks smiled even when his spirit was numb with sorrow. His shining lips doubly commended the honey of his words, and wherever he turned his eyes, his look announced the serenity of his mind. His brow had a waxen beauty and the kind of whiteness that, having endured the sun's rays, has drawn its colour from the sky. His nostrils were naturally formed with such grace that a painter portraying bodies in images could not rival them. His hands were smooth and rounded, his fingers long, so that even a foreigner would be glad to receive something from them. His tall stature was seemly. In his limbs it prefigured the eminence of the dignity that was to follow, yet it did not exceed the measure of a most graceful height.

Some malicious interpreter may claim that it was out of place to mention the charm of the flesh in a man of such virtues. But it is planted in that ancient root of the heavenly commandments that the bodies of priests must be examined with careful scrutiny. Nothing weak or deformed may be found in them, nothing too much or too little. No foul surface ingrained with blemishes may disgrace the skin, and no broken hand, broken foot or hump may make a bishop unworthy of the altar. The teacher of the Gentiles, the chosen vessel, also cries out that a man must be clean to come to such an office, and he is believed to have meant the purity not only of the soul but also of the body. Above all, the One who commands that the deformed and the weak be kept from his offerings is found gladly to admit those who are pleasing in many ways. This is especially so for one in whom the radiance of the soul surpasses the brightness of the limbs, and whose earthly beauty is natural and not helped by any artifice.

I have now touched briefly on these things, which ought not to be omitted, so that this immense man might be presented, in deed and in countenance, to everyone who comes to know him. Let me pass to matters told of the worshippers of our God which deserve no small praise. His speech was suited to teaching and shaped to win favour. Even then he was skilled at intercession. He was full of authority when rebuking individuals and most sweet, with a needful charm, when exhorting anyone. His voice was resonant and seasoned with the sap of manly elegance, yet it was neither boorish and rustic nor broken and gradually sunk from masculine firmness. Whoever saw him before he had crossed the threshold of any rank believed he had already passed through all the honours that were to follow.

Such he was when he reached his eighteenth year. In that year he was ordained to the rank next below the Levites, and a boy joined the assemblies of elders. Many were amazed, but they were outsiders, who weighed his character together with the immaturity of his age. Those who knew him believed this dignity had come late. The venerable Bishop Crispinus was a stranger to favouritism. He held to his strictness with unbending severity, and nothing but a good conscience ever moved him to show favour. So he soothed the young man in his feelings while he bit him with his look, and beneath a stern brow he nursed a hidden affection for his disciple. The father fed on his pupil's admirable conduct and delighted his eyes in all his actions. Yet the young man stayed no more than two years in the order of the subdiaconate. Raised by the leaps of his merits, he sprang upward, for his rich soul would not let itself be held long within the narrow bounds of a modest honour. His conscience hastened toward the dignity of the Levites, which his wishes had never presumed. His way of life demanded what his desires knew nothing of.

Around the close and end of that rank, however, I would like to touch briefly on one of his deeds. There is an estate called Summias, set in a place where the greedy bite of the Po's current gnaws at the earthen bank. The winding, serpentine river grants to one owner in a lump what it steals from another, so that a neighbour's loss becomes the next man's gain. A certain Burco was contending with the clergy over this estate in an old lawsuit. The quarrel was very aged, older than anyone could reckon, and to settle it he was sent while still a boy. He was chosen because he could both bravely meet the claims brought against them and temper, with mature counsel, those they were to bring. Yet contention, the mother of all crimes, produced what it usually produces. As the talk and the quarrel went on, Burco, who indulged his own malice with sordid assent [?], committed the supreme crime without any fear. He struck the holy man with a club so that blood at once gushed out. But the young man, most ready, held back his anger. He did not boil over, provoked by hope of revenge, but instead soothed the troubled and astonished attacker with the gentlest words. At once Burco's mother Capraria came running, crying that the atrocity of the deed had made her wretched and robbed her of her son. You would have thought she was tossed about at her child's funeral by that lamentation which, at the deaths of loved ones, drives all reason away. Wailing, the mother kissed the footprints of the most holy youth and cried 'Spare him!' to one whom no force had ever driven to indignation. But he forbade her pleading, lest by her begging she stir up resentment against him, and lest she burden him, who did not deserve it, with the weight of an honour paid to him. Suddenly the city was in uproar, and the minds of all the Christians turned to fury. Burco was demanded for execution, and in all that great crowd no one was found calm except the man who had suffered the injury. The excellent bishop wept over the young man's wounds, while the disciple rejoiced in his sufferings. He made satisfaction to each person on behalf of the man thought to be his enemy. In doing so he neither boastfully sought glory by sparing him nor broke the heavenly commandments by taking revenge.

Soon afterward he was raised to the insignia of the diaconate. He reached his twentieth year with his face not yet properly bearded. He was troubled by the novelty of the honour he had received, though he could already have filled the role of a Christian leader. Out of modesty he avoided the gaze of individuals, though the whole city watched him as a kind of sign of salvation. Meanwhile the bishop mentioned above entrusted to his control the whole substance of the church's household and the wealth of his poor. Before the episcopate came, he wanted to learn what kind of bishop he was preparing for times to come. Envy is hardly ever restrained toward those about whom even the slightest suspicion of succession has been sown. Yet the holy father believed that whatever favour was withheld from the young man was lost to himself. Some things in him he wanted to be his own, others he wanted to be greater still. But by his daily progress the young man surpassed the wishes of even this father, most eager in his prayers. And he was indeed his father: his womb, made fruitful by the seed of the heavenly word, had brought forth the son he conceived through the gospel. What shall I say of the chastity of my young man? In him chastity had set up its house, and continence had sunk its roots deep. He knew he was a man only through enduring toil, and he was not aware of having flesh except when he remembered that he would die. Yet whenever bodily appetite mocked him with images in his dreams, as I learned from him, he at once ran with full eagerness to holy vigils, unbroken fasts and the need to stand for very long periods. The warrior right hand of his soul reduced his flesh by these struggles to such a state that afterward it had to be given some help out of necessity. Yet when his frail body had been restored, he did not indulge in leisure. He used reading as his rest and took up the instruments of venerable books in place of comforts. He could recite from memory what he had read through once. And lest he be thought to have flown over the path of the divine Scriptures by mere speed of words, he painted with his actions the page he had read. If a prophet was in his hands, you would see the reader prophesying once the book was laid aside. If he had gone over the volumes of the Old Testament, he walked as a worthy imitator of Moses, as though the columns of Israel were following him through the desert. If Scripture, as guide, had revealed the apostolic milk of words and the honey of the Lord's passion, which season the severity of the law, words sweeter than honeycomb at once flowed from his mouth. In short, his life bore the stamp of whatever the books had taught.

He governed the church's household in such a way that he neither drained the stores entrusted to him by immoderate lavishness nor drew hatred on himself by mean stinginess. Even then he was rehearsing for the contests of intercession. Wherever the bishop's command sent him to bring relief to the wretched, he obtained the favour with such art in pleading that very many felt their cases had gained by the bishop not coming in person. Popular affection for him grew day by day, and a love born of sound judgement was heaped up by great successes. People longed to see the episcopate in him, though no one wished for the death of the man who had raised him. He himself was not touched by even a breath of this opinion. He thought it enough for his advancement if he always served in good esteem. Later, feeble old age, forever complaining of its infirmities, seized the venerable Bishop Crispinus. He was then held up by the young man's hands and raised himself leaning on his embrace. The young man was his foot, his eye, his right hand. Through his service the bishop saw whatever he wanted done carried out before he had given the order, for good minds sense in advance the wishes of those they serve with integrity. Such was he in the diaconate, which he began at twenty and in which he completed eight years. At that time the church of Ticinum was flourishing with a good harvest of clergy. There were heavenly men, and he, beginning from perfection, went before them. Silvester was archdeacon then, a man thoroughly proven in the old training of the disciplines. There was the most distinguished priest Bonosus, as noble in holiness as in blood, a Gaul by descent but a native of heaven. There were others too, many in number and outstanding in virtue. I mention them because one who is preferred only to the wretched deserves little praise.

Toward the end of his life, which the holy bishop foresaw in spirit, he went to the neighbouring city of Milan, where the offspring of nobles had grown up like a harvest of pure noble birth. He sought them out for a visit, and the man of God addressed them with words like these: 'See, my sons, age now compels me toward my passing. The earth now calls back its own original particle under its claim. I commend the city, I commend the church, I commend this man. To his labour and grace I owe it that up to this time, when I am very aged and feeble [?]... His bodily strength and strength of soul have borne my weakness without disdain. I have walked on his feet, held things with his hands, seen with his eyes and given orders with his speech. To onlookers we seemed two, while through concord one was made out of two.' These words, spoken to the illustrious Rusticius, sank deep into him. He was highly practised in every kind of speaking, and he began with this address: 'We know, holy father, we know, and we have seen on deep reflection, that this young man should not be judged by the immaturity of his age. Men of weighty counsel should not treat his tender years as an obstacle. A man proven by a grey-haired integrity of character deserves double praise if his boyish body obeys the venerable command of his mind. But live on yourself, live on as the example and pattern of good works, and add in him still richer fruits of shining conduct, if they can grow any further.' With these words he fell silent. The most devout bishop thanked him for his goodwill, because he shared his own estimate of his disciple. He said farewell, departed and returned to Ticinum as if hastening to his tomb. After some days had passed he was overcome by jaundice and exchanged the light of our world for the dwelling above.

At once the consensus of all good men was drawn to him, and immediately a great crowd gathered throughout the city. The bishop-to-be was snatched from funeral lament into the people's joy. He wept without restraint in grief at his father's death, for the gladness of the mingled crowd did not let him pay the tears that were due. He resisted as far as he could and, now imitating the apostle, kept crying out that he was unworthy. But the love of all for him rose the higher because, in that great multitude, he alone called himself unworthy. Why should I say more, when I cannot explain everything? The neighbouring cities joined in their zeal, and so great a gathering was drawn together that you would think the bishop of the whole world was being ordained. He was led to Milan, still resisting and promising great gifts if he were let go, though he would not promise even the smallest gift to be made bishop. He was consecrated with every solemnity, in the presence of all. The world exulted at the insignia of so holy an ordination. The inhabitants of other cities rejoiced with such celebration that you would think he had received the priestly fillets to benefit them in particular. Yet voracious envy consumed some inhabitants of great cities. They resented that the narrow town of Ticinum had deserved so great a bishop, while among them only the titles of metropolitan pride protected their bishops.

When the day of his consecration was over, he returned to Ticinum. He called together all the priests and ministers, and he instructed and encouraged them with words like these: 'Dearest brothers, as I totter, unripe, at these beginnings, the weight of your judgement and of the dignity I have received has overwhelmed me. Yet I remember that I owe much to your goodwill, since you have conferred so much on me. I would rather obey you than command you. Through this office I have changed my role, but I have not given up the will to serve. Be peaceable and of one mind, and share my burden with me, for a load becomes easy to carry when the necks of many support it. I promise with all humility to keep communion with you, and that no one will be able to offend me except by offending our God as well. Guard chastity, the source of good works. And do not think it an insult that a boy calls aged men and priests to preserve continence and integrity, for it is conduct, not years, that shows youth or old age. Look into the inner workings of my conduct, and if you find anything unworthy, restrain it. Let no one fear to admonish the head of the church if he finds him going astray.' Having said this he fell silent. All rose and spoke in unison, as though from earlier rehearsal, yet with a spontaneous voice: 'Hail, most proven father, hail, matchless bishop! The choice of all perceived that you were good, but your words testify that you are the best. In our minds you grow in holy merits, and the light of your works reveals you beyond what our opinion of you had reached.' When these few words had been spoken, they all received a gift and departed.

Soon the blessed bishop dictated with his own mouth the laws by which he would hold himself. First, he resolved never to bathe, lest the baths, which are friendlier to filth, break down the brightness of his soul and the strength of the inner man. Next, he had decided never to take a midday meal. But the pressure of visitors might violate the resolve he had made, and his purpose might be harmed by clouds of boasting or a reputation for avarice. So he settled instead never to take supper, so that the change of hours would give him a time for eating once a day. He made himself content with the cheapest foods, and nothing in the preparation of dishes could offend his nose and palate except what was seasoned with spices. He fed on meals of vegetables and legumes, but he took neither to the point of fullness. He took a very little wine, and even that small amount only because he remembered the apostle's advice to guard against weakness of the stomach. He resolved to set out earlier than everyone else in any dreadful weather, so that the bishop, arriving at the church ahead of the lectors, would give them a pattern for keeping vigil. Once he reached the precincts of the altar, he determined that no necessity would draw him away before the solemn rites were completed. He resolved to stand with his feet together until the mystic work was finished, so that the moisture of his footprints marked his place and showed it to those looking from afar. He took such care over intercessions that he believed he himself inflicted on the wretched any harm he had negligently allowed anyone to inflict. In times of leisure he trained his body to endure toil, so that it would be equal to necessity. This was the practical rule of living, the doctrine of discipline, that he set for himself. He undertook it, kept it and fulfilled it.

Soon report spread news of his holy way of life throughout the whole world. Report is usually rather slow where glorious deeds are concerned, but it did not keep silent here. It carried the news to the ears of Ricimer, who at that time governed the state, holding the reins second only to the emperor Anthemius. For once the emperor had been established at Rome, envy, which divides rulers, sowed the seed of offence between them, and equal rank became a cause of discord. Such fury and dissension had arisen that they were preparing war against each other. Besides the goads that the origin of their anger supplied of itself, the quarrel was fed by the counsel of those around them. The condition of imperilled Italy was tottering. While it waited for dangers to come, it was afflicted more heavily by the dangers themselves. Meanwhile the nobility of Liguria assembled before the patrician Ricimer, who was residing at Milan at the time. On bended knee and prostrate on the ground, they begged for peace between the rulers. They prayed that, so that both sides might cease from offence, one of them would offer an opening for reconciliation. Why should I spin out more? Ricimer was softened, and, moved by the weeping of many, he promised that he was willing to restore concord. "But who," he said, "is best fitted to take up the burden of this embassy? Who will bear the charge of so great a task? Who is there who can call back an angry Galatian, and an emperor at that? For whoever does not bound his anger by natural moderation always gets the upper hand, even when he is being managed [?]." Then all answered with one voice: "Only let your assent incline toward peace. We have a man who was recently called to the episcopate of the city of Ticinum. Even raging beasts bow their necks to him. Whatever he comes to ask of anyone, the favour is offered before he can make his request. His face is like his life. Any Catholic and Roman can revere him, and even a little Greek would surely love him if he were found worthy to see him. And if we come to his speech, no Thessalian enchanter with his violent spells and his fingering of words could ever call forth dread asps as surely as he wrests the fulfilment of his petition even from those who mean to refuse. Once he begins to speak, the hearer's verdict hangs on his will. Whoever has resolved to refuse will lose that right if he gives him the chance to plead." Then the patrician Ricimer replied: "Report has brought this man you describe to my attention as glorious. What I admire all the more is that, although everyone praises him, his new rank, which usually abounds in enemies through envy, has brought him none. Go, then, and ask the man of God to make the journey, and add my prayers to yours." They left the council and at once made for Ticinum, where they explained the matter. With tears they begged blessed Epiphanius to undertake this labour. So as not to lessen the favour by tormenting his sons with lengthy pleading, he anticipated the wishes of those who asked. Yet he addressed them thus: "The necessity of so great a matter calls for the weight of a thoroughly proven man, and an untried bearer staggers under a heavy load. Even so, I will not deny the affection I owe to my country." He said this briefly, for he was sparing of speech, and then went to the patrician Ricimer. Ricimer saw him and chose him in the same moment.

So, with the commission of the embassy entrusted to him, he set out for Rome. What hardships he endured on that journey, or what mighty works he performed, I pass over, hastening on to greater things. But as soon as he entered the gates of that city, report, which had made him known in his absence, began to point him out with its finger. At once all eyes turned to him. Minds were stunned and amazed that his appearance, the sign of his holiness, should claim such reverence for itself. Any of the powerful confessed himself guilty of an unpardonable fault if he had only [?] embraced his knees. A shout rose to heaven. No one counted him among mortals, for they saw that all the good things of heavenly grace were found in him. Word was brought to the emperor Anthemius that a bishop of Liguria had come on an embassy, a man whom no one, however rich in eloquence, could adequately describe. But he said: "Ricimer contends with me by cunning art even in his embassies. He sends such men as can win over by entreaty those whom he provokes with injuries. Nevertheless, bring the man of God to me. If he asks for what is possible, I will grant it. If he asks for what is difficult, I will beg him not to take it amiss when I decline. Yet I doubt whether Ricimer will obtain what he demands from me, for I know him to be a man without restraint in his wishes, who keeps no bounds of reason when he proposes terms. But let the bishop he has sent come and show us the face that has been praised for so long." The palace officials went out through the whole city, and the bishop kept hearing: "Please come; you are asked for."

The venerable bishop, approved by every age, went in and was granted leave to speak. With the radiance of his revered appearance he outshone the insignia of fleeting power, the purple and the glittering gems, for he drew every eye to himself as if the emperor were not there. Nevertheless he opened the door of his mouth with this address: "Venerable prince, the supreme ordinance of the heavenly Lord has arranged that the one entrusted with the care of so great a commonwealth should acknowledge, through the teaching of the Catholic faith, that God is both the author and the lover of mercy. Through him the arms of peace break the fury of war, and concord, treading on the necks of pride, overcomes what strength cannot master. So it was that David was made praiseworthy by his readiness to spare his enemy rather than by any intent of vengeance. So too the perfect kings and lords of the ages have learned by a heavenly art to show indulgence to suppliants. For whoever exalts his rule by mercy possesses the likeness of the dominion on high. Relying on this judgment, your Italy, or rather the patrician Ricimer, has sent my insignificance to plead, confident beyond doubt that a Roman will give to God as a gift the peace that even a barbarian begs for. It will be a triumph that truly adorns your annals if you conquer without bloodshed. At the same time, I do not know what kind of warfare could be braver than to fight against anger and to load the shame of a most ferocious Goth with benefits. For one who until now was ashamed to plead is struck the harder if he obtains what he asks. Next, the uncertain outcome of war must be weighed. In it, even if you should prevail in the contest [?], your realm will be robbed of whatever both sides have lost. For whatever is with Ricimer is safe if he is a friend, since through the patrician himself it belongs to us. Consider also that the one who offers peace first sets his cause on a sound course."

Here the admirable bishop came to the end of his speech. Then the emperor raised his eyes and saw that everyone's gaze had left him and that all faces were drawn toward the bishop, whom he himself could not stop admiring. Drawing his words from a deep sigh, he began thus: "Holy bishop, I have a grievance against Ricimer that I cannot unfold. The very great benefits I gave him have done no good. I even joined him to my family line, a thing that cannot be said without shame to my reign and my blood. In this I gave way to love of the commonwealth, though it might seem to show hatred toward my own. Which of the ancient emperors before me ever did such a thing, that among the gifts which had to be given to a skin-clad Goth a daughter should be offered for the common peace? I did not know how to spare my own blood while I preserved the blood of others. Yet let no one believe that this was done out of fear for myself. In my great concern for the safety of all, I alone have never learned to fear for myself. For I hold it as well established that an emperor loses the praise of his valour if he does not fear for the safety of others. But let me lay bare his designs plainly to your reverence. The more often I heaped greater gifts on Ricimer, the more dangerous an enemy he showed himself. What wars he has prepared against the commonwealth! What strength the fury of foreign nations has gained through him! And finally, where he could [not?] harm me himself, he still supplied the kindling for harm. Shall I give peace to such a man? Shall I tolerate this enemy within, cloaked in the garment of friendship, when not even the bonds of kinship held him to the pact of concord? To know an adversary's mind is a great safeguard. Indeed, to have seen through an enemy at once is to have overcome him. Hatreds that are detected always lose the stings they nursed while hidden. But if in all this your reverence comes forward as both surety and mediator, you who can discover wicked plans by spiritual searching and correct them once found, I dare not refuse the peace that you also ask. Finally, if the cunning of his usual craft deceives even you, then let the fight be taken up by one already wounded [?]. Yet I commit and entrust myself and the state of the commonwealth to your hands. The favour I had resolved to refuse to Ricimer, even if he pleaded with me prostrate in person, I grant at once through you. After deep deliberation I consider my own interest in this matter, if amid the uncertain wanderings of the storm I steer the ship by the direction of a good helmsman. For who would presume to refuse a favour to you when you ask, when it ought to have been offered before you asked?" So spoke the emperor. And the venerable bishop said: "Thanks be to almighty God, who has planted his peace in the mind of the emperor, whom he willed to be the vicar of his power among mortals, after the pattern of the dominion on high."

After this brief exchange he also received an oath from Anthemius to make the concord secure. Then he departed, hastening to return to Liguria, for the season of the Lord's resurrection was at hand. In that season, when bodies have been worn down by the cross of fasting, the joyful spirit grows warm again though the flesh is cold. And as death is conquered by our Redeemer's dying, the soul is fed on the food of faithful hope. When he left Rome, Easter was twenty days away. Yet he made the journey with such speed that on the fourteenth day he entered Ticinum unexpectedly, ahead of any news of his coming. Indeed, he left very many of his companions behind on the road, because they could bear neither his abstinence nor his toil. People who were still waiting for the arrival of so great a bishop came running together to see him already settled at home, when they had understood that he had not yet left Rome. The jubilation of the joyful city was reported to the astonished Ricimer, and all cried with one voice that peace had been made. The provinces rejoiced without bounds. It is the way of men to value what is restored to them more highly than what was never lost at all, and so the concord recovered after strife was all the sweeter, and so was the peace that came when it had almost been despaired of. The reverend bishop was invited to show himself to the people of Milan, who had long been waiting to see him. But he did not want his presence to seem like a demand for thanks as if they were owed him, and so he declined their visits under a plausible pretext. So with the passing of time and the daily success of his labours, the merit of his life was doubled in him. He had a younger sister named Honorata, no less devout than he. It would take long to recount her life through every kind of virtue, but it is praise enough to call her a sister worthy of so great a man. He consecrated her in the very year he returned from the embassy. Yet, as though her holy nature were not enough, he entrusted her to be schooled in heavenly disciplines to a certain Luminosa, a woman of astonishing holiness and singular example. It might perhaps be fitting to recount the eminence of her birth, had her life not been more distinguished than her blood. She was such that even he who entrusted his own sister to her for instruction believed he had something to learn from her. In a short time the pledge the bishop had placed with her blossomed, and she brought the laden young plants to the ripeness of good fruit. Meanwhile the venerable bishop advanced swiftly along the path of life he had set himself. He devoted himself to almsgiving without holding back, and he commended his gifts to those who received them with a most gracious face and spirit. Even someone to whom he had given only the favour of a word by no means thought he went away empty-handed, for it was the greatest reward just to have seen such a bishop. Day by day his fame grew through glorious successes, and it filled almost the whole world with his praise.

Then, when Ricimer and Anthemius had died, Olybrius succeeded, and he met his last day at the very start of his reign. After him Glycerius was called to the throne. How much the bishop did with him for the welfare of many I cut short for the sake of brevity. At the holy man's plea, Glycerius pardoned the injury that men under his rule had done to his mother, for the bishop was held in even higher reverence by him than by his predecessor. After him Nepos came to the throne. Then a dispute arose between him and the Goths, the nurslings of Toulouse, whom King Euric governed with iron rule. Scorning the new emperor, they did not cease to attack the borders that the Italian empire had extended beyond the Gallic Alps. Nepos, for his part, did not want their wicked presumption to become custom, and so he was determined to defend more firmly the bounds of rule that God had entrusted to him. From this, the kindling of quarrels began to blaze up on both sides. Neither side would lay aside its swollen pride in its eagerness to win, and so the cause of discord kept growing. The most blessed man had already reached the eighth year of his episcopate when suddenly a desire to end the dispute filled the mind of Nepos. He wished to drive out the poison of rivalry, so that charity might preserve between the kings what arms could scarcely protect. The lights of Liguria were summoned to council, men of mature judgment, by whose deliberation the tottering condition of the commonwealth might revive and its lost stability be restored to its ancient height. At the emperor's command as many leaders came together for the discussion as could be found. Talk turned to arranging an embassy. The minds and eyes of all were turned to the most blessed man Epiphanius, and the opinions of all were as though spoken from one mouth and one heart. Why say more? The soldier of Christ joyfully embraced the chance to labour and anticipated the outcome in hope. Confident in his judgment of the business, he sought the best way to carry it out [?]. Relying on the protection of heavenly power, he weighed, undertook, and accomplished a task that had been almost given up for lost and was very difficult. I could not set out in order the hardships and trials of this journey, not even if words poured from me through watering channels in the rivers of a hundred tongues. From the time he left the town of Ticinum until he reached his destination, he doubled the fatigue of the road by this practice. Sometimes, mindful of the exhaustion of the pack animals, they arrived early at the lodging of the next stage. Then, besides continual psalmody and persistent reading, none of which he did except standing, he would choose a retreat enclosed by the leaves of the woods. There the interlaced arms of the trees wove a homely night, which the sun alone did not know as it fled through the dark shade, and natural grace spread a couch of green turf. Stretched out there in prayer, with ceaseless weeping he watered a rainless earth with the showers of his eyes. Those fields, which could not be fertile with crops, were made fertile by an abundance of prayers.

Mortifying himself with such exercises, he entered the city of Toulouse, where King Euric was then living. Report had gone before him and had already told the Gauls what kind of man he was, above all the bishops of that region, who in their astonishment were busy making close inquiry about the newcomers. At that time there was also a man named Leo, who both directed and judged the king's counsels and had already won more than one prize in declamation for his eloquence. With the greatest joy he made the bishop's arrival publicly known. The bishop was summoned at once to be presented to the king. He went in to him without delay, saw him, greeted him, and addressed him: "Astonishing prince of the earth, the fame of your valour makes you terrible in the ears of many, and your swords, with which you press your neighbours by continual devastation, reap a kind of harvest of hostile growth. Yet the fierce ambition of war wins you no favour from the heavenly Godhead, nor does the sword protect the borders of an empire if the Lord of heaven is offended. Remember that you have a King whose pleasure you must consider. When he was carrying into heaven the humanity he had assumed, he commended peace to his disciples as the gift of an immense inheritance, repeating the admonition again and again. We must keep his command, especially since we know that a man whom indignation has conquered cannot be called brave. Next we should weigh this: no one guards his own more carefully than the one who does not covet what belongs to others. Therefore Nepos, to whom divine ordinance has entrusted the rule of Italy, has sent us to obtain this from you: that minds be brought back to good faith, and that lands which border one another be joined by the law of love. Though he does not fear conflict, he is the first to desire concord. You know as well as we do the boundary by which these neighbouring domains have been marked off from of old, and with what patient service your people once bore the rulers of ours. Let it suffice that he who deserved to be called master has chosen, or at least allows, to be called friend." So spoke that most distinguished man Epiphanius.

Euric broke into some murmur in his native tongue, and the calm of his face showed that the bishop's exhortations had softened him. Leo, whom I named above, was so struck with wonder at the bishop's address that he believed minds could be conquered by words of this kind, if it is lawful to say so, even if he were asking for something unjust. Yet the king is said to have spoken thus through an interpreter: "The breastplate hardly ever leaves my chest, a round bronze shield constantly encloses my hand, and a defence of iron guards my side. Yet I have found a man who can conquer me, armed as I am, with words. Those who say that the Romans have no shield or spears in their tongues are mistaken. For they know how to drive back the words we send, and how to aim the words they direct into the innermost heart. So I will do what you ask, venerable father, because the person of the envoy weighs more with me than the power of the one who sent him. Receive my pledge now, and promise on behalf of Nepos that he will keep the concord unbroken, since for you to have promised is to have sworn." When this had been said and the bond of the agreement concluded, the revered bishop said farewell and departed. At once a crowd of petitioners was sent to him, asking him to attend the king's banquet the next day. But he had already learned that the king's priests continually polluted his feasts. He excused himself, saying that it was not his custom ever to eat at other people's tables, and that he would rather set out on the day after next. He made haste to carry out this decision. He left Toulouse with so many people escorting him that when our bishop departed the city seemed almost deserted. For in a short time he had bound so many to himself by sincere charity that those whom necessity forced to remain in their homeland wept as if they were captives. Returning from there, he visited each of the places of holy dwellings. He went to the Medianae islands, the Stoechades, Lero, and level Lérins itself, the nurse of the loftiest mountains. From all of them he gathered each little flower of their life, so that the spark of good seed might implant them in him, and the tree, laden with heavenly fruit, might bring them to the season of ripeness. Meanwhile the light the Italians had awaited was restored to them, and with the return of the matchless bishop a gleaming radiance shone out across the clear sky. Long desired, he entered Ticinum and reported to Nepos the success of his completed embassy. As his praises mounted, the humility in him grew in equal measure.

So while this worker of Christ our God was training himself in such disciplines and labors, behold, the enemy who knows no rest and commits every crime piled up great new sorrows and looked for sufferings with which to assail this most upright man. He raised an army against the patrician Orestes and, secretly undermining, sowed the crimes of discord. With the hope of revolution he stirred up the minds of desperate men. He lifted Odoacer to the ambition of ruling, and so that this disaster would happen in the city of Ticinum, he lured Orestes there by trust in its fortifications. The bishop was found in the city with all his household. There was a great rush through the city, and the madness for plunder blazed up: everywhere grief, everywhere fear, and many an image of death. He ran about anxiously. Any man whose wealth had become better known through long and loyal friendships was demanded for torture. Some set fire to houses that were about to fall; others demanded the death of the very master for whose safety they had gathered to fight. They ran to the church house, burning with every fire of plunder, for they suspected that the man they had seen giving away so much was hiding immense sums. For shame! Crude barbarians searched the earth for treasures that he had sent ahead to the secret places of heaven. His holy sister too was seized and led away from him to the lot of captivity. All the households of the nobles were separated from their own, and the most glorious lady Luminosa was held under the same hard condition. O grief! Both churches were burned by enemy flames, and the whole city blazed like a funeral pyre. The voices of everyone could be heard looking for the bishop. No one thought of his own danger while the greater part of their safety was cut off from them. And though the confused mob raged for the death of each person, honor was still paid to him even among the swords. For right away there were no captives left wherever he could see them. Before the deadly light of that day slipped into evening, he rescued his venerable sister. By his pleading he also freed a great many citizens before they felt the chains of that harshest condition, above all the matrons, for whom a longer stay in such a plight could have been crueler still. In the end the city, which the barbarian horde was cutting down, rose again, held up by the help of a single very strong column. The army was not as able to destroy as the person of one bishop was able to restore. But when Orestes had been captured and killed near the city of Placentia, the frenzy of plunder died down.

After him Odoacer was raised to the kingship and began to honor this distinguished man with such regard that he outdid all his predecessors in his attentions to him. Meanwhile, so that the houses of God would not lie long buried in ashes, the glorious bishop resolved to rebuild before he had the funds or the means to prepare the work. He did not fear to raise very costly buildings without a store of coin. He knew well the apostle's teaching that those who seek the heavenly kingdom always have an unfailing income in abundance, and that one whom poverty does not crush in his will to give always gives from fullness. For he used to say: "Means rarely desert a rich spirit, and it is very hard for abundance to follow a man who is a beggar in mind." The work on the greater church had already reached its completion, and the building had been adorned with the marks of its dedication, when suddenly the colonnaded wall of the other church was thrown down by a push from the cunning serpent. He wanted to see whether he could overthrow the bishop with trouble upon trouble. But the bishop rose up all the more vigorously so as not to give way to his evils, and at once, without any sign of distress, he set about rebuilding it with full eagerness. Everyone was struck with great wonder, for the workmen fell from the very dome of the church together with a huge scaffold, yet none of them was lamed in the leg or maimed in any part of the body. It was plain to everyone that this had happened through the bishop's prayers: the collapse held up its own mass, and the stones were kept from falling. By the astonishing pace of his management the work was brought to completion. For once the greater church was finished, he began the repairs, and people who had not yet heard that the work was begun saw the house of God swiftly risen to the height of its former soundness. When he had quickly completed these things, divine favor soon showed itself in him. For in the course of that same year a great crowd of demons began to cry out from the bodies they possessed that they were being driven out by whips and terrible torments at the command of the bishop Epiphanius. With a brief prayer poured out in tears he sent them off to the farthest ends of the earth, and as they howled in various voices he drove them on by the authority of his merits. Yet though he did such things continually through the grace of Christ, he took for himself nothing of the winds of presumption. For the power of good merit is taken away from those in whom confidence in their own goodness has bred arrogance.

Meanwhile, so that he would not seem to have adorned the city with churches alone, he provided useful relief for its weary inhabitants. He sent an embassy to Odoacer and obtained a five-year remission of fiscal taxes. In dividing these benefits among individuals he kept himself so scrupulously in check that no one received less than the man at whose request they had been granted. While this was going on, however, the long-stored malice of Pelagius, who was praetorian prefect at that time, boiled over to the ruin of the landowners of Liguria. Through enormous compulsory purchases he doubled taxes that were already very heavy, and imposed a double burden when even a single one could not be borne. So the crowd of the oppressed soon flocked to the holy man. He gladly seized the opportunity to help, and for the need of all he eagerly went, asked, and obtained. But why do I vainly long to describe each kind and form of his labors, when affection attempts what ability cannot set forth, and the narrowness of speech sets a limit for those who would think on larger things? Yet the holy man's most sacred wish was that, though he did countless things, either none or only a few of his praises should be mentioned. So whatever my poor tongue has failed to tell, I leave to the minds of those who hear and read.

After many embassies to King Odoacer, which the force of his pleading carried through, by the ordering of heaven's rule King Theodoric came into Italy with an immense host of his forces. When Theodoric was already established at Milan, this most upright man went out to meet him. That most excellent of kings looked at him with the eyes of his heart and weighed our bishop in the usual balance of his judgment, and he found in him the weight of every virtue. He measured his integrity as if with a builder's lines against the plumb line of his own mind, and he spoke of him to his men in these words: "Here is a man whose like the whole East does not have, whom to have seen is a reward, with whom to live is security. As long as he is safe, the city of Ticinum is surrounded by a mighty wall, which no force of attackers can overwhelm and which no shot from a Balearic sling can clear. If any need arises amid the waves of battle, it is safe to leave mother and family with him and to go to war unencumbered."

Meanwhile a desire for change inflamed the treacherous minds of the army that had surrendered. Its leader was Tufa, a man long stained with the infamy of a deserter, who planned to go back over to the desperate side with a huge multitude. When King Theodoric learned of this through his princely vigilance, he at once gathered all that force which the whole East had scarcely been able to withstand and withdrew into the narrow confines of the city of Ticinum. You would have seen the city teeming with crowds of households, the roofs of huge houses cut down into tiny huts. You would have seen vast buildings moved from their foundations, and the very ground unable to hold so dense a throng of inhabitants.

Amid all this, that man, so practiced in good works, whose greatness of spirit opened access to everyone, judged that an opportune time had been offered him to spread the sails of his kindness to a full south wind, and to reach the harbor of glory on a favorable voyage through his acquaintance with various peoples and the renown of his deeds. And first of all he achieved something that no writings of the ancients and no annals in books record of anyone, something that a narrator would affirm with astonishment and a reader accept with wonder. Living among a most shrewd people, past whom no breath of suspicion slips, in uncertain times, when fear of danger stirs even gentle hearts against anyone at all, he proved so loyal to them that he held their enemies bound to him in complete affection, and among warring princes he alone enjoyed the peace of both. Whatever was given him by one, he put to the benefit of the other; and by the reverence due his person and by his gentleness he so tempered the giver's mind that it was in no way inflamed if even an enemy received some of his bounty through the bishop. He was the one man with whom even combatants kept concord, and whose peace wars did not disturb. Now if we come to the fact that with daily kindness he fed the very plunderers, and inside the city supplied the necessities of life to those who outside had laid waste his estates with continual devastation! At one and the same time he refreshed so many thousands of men, though they demanded different things: he soothed them with kindness, calmed them with his words, and fed them with gifts. If anyone's children and wife had been seized by enemies intercepting them from either side, they were at once returned to their own at the price of his pleading, when no outpouring of gold could have ransomed them. He was most acceptable to the king and venerable above all holy men, so that whatever Romans the license of war had made captives of the king's men, the king soon restored to the bishop, whom he knew to be enriched only by the freedom of others. Moreover, I could not count how many columns of subjugated people he restored to their own soil, or how many he arranged to be spared from harassment. And if I were to recount the insolence of enemies he endured, the assaults he suffered, and the courage with which he scorned the storms of the wicked, my tongue would not be equal to telling it. One is glad to pick out certain things, when everything one reports is to be admired. Under such a cross he spent three years, revealing the secrets of his sorrows to God alone, from whom he asked for hidden help.

After the Goths had departed from there, the city of Ticinum was handed over to the Rugians, men monstrous in every kind of savagery, whom a fierce and bitter violence of spirit drove to daily crimes. They thought a day was lost if some chance had let it pass without a crime. Yet the most blessed bishop soothed them with the honey of his words, so that their savage hearts submitted to the bishop's authority, and those whose breasts we know had always been given over to hatred learned to love. Through his merit their natural perversity was changed, as the root of an affection foreign to them was grafted into their uncivilized minds. Who would believe without great astonishment that the Rugians, who scarcely deign to obey kings, loved and feared a bishop, and a Catholic and a Roman one at that? He spent nearly two full years with them, and in such a way that they parted from him in tears, even though they were going home to their parents and families.

But after that wretched and deadly war was over, and victory went to the man after whose triumph no one saw a sword drawn from its scabbard, who ended his army's arrogance along with the battle, the venerable bishop at once set about planning the restoration of his city. With the deliberation of spiritual counsel he made provision to fill it as soon as possible with worthy inhabitants. Although through his prayers no whirlwind of that worldly storm had driven it to devastation, he believed it would hardly be enough if, after the ruin of all the cities of Liguria, Ticinum rejoiced content with its own natives alone. He began to gather certain choice flowers among the citizens of the neighboring cities, and like a diligent gardener to carry seedlings already proven to his own gardens, so that he, a thrifty and capable owner, might pick from them the finest fruit.

Meanwhile a sudden resolve took hold of the mind of the most excellent King Theodoric: to grant the right of Roman liberty only to those whose proven loyalty had joined them to his side. Those whom some necessity had kept apart from him he ordered to be stripped of all freedom to make wills and to dispose of their property and wishes. When this decision was proclaimed and the laws had been trampled underfoot for so many by such a law, all Italy lay under a lamentable suspension of justice. Once more people turned to the man who with a healing hand had been accustomed to help public wounds, and whose fountain had often quenched the heat of misfortune. When he said that he alone could not bear so great a burden, the venerable Laurentius, bishop of Milan, was asked as well. They set out together and arrived together at Ravenna, where they were received with reverence. Once the opportunity to plead was opened to them, blessed Laurentius thought it necessary that the chance to speak be given above all to the man whose feet had been worn by the laborious path of frequent embassies, and who, hurrying along such roads, had more than once been made shaggy with the dust of camps. He began the public petition with this speech: "Most invincible prince, if I were to recount in order how greatly divine favor has raised your good fortune through countless successes, you would recognize that you, who are sparing in your prayers, have always received from our God greater benefits than you remember wishing for. It is enough, however, to tell one of them, but the greatest: that we plead the cases of your servants before you as prince in the very place where your enemy used to rejoice in possessing this throne. You owe much to Christ our Redeemer. He himself has given you those for whom we ask. We must take care not to offend the giver of the gift by failing to love what he has given. I have held back my confidence too long. I would go through one by one the things I have heard told and have seen come to you by the help of God. You know what you promised you would do when you were pressed by the densest wedges of enemies and the blare of the hostile trumpet sounded around the walls of the little city of Ticinum, when adversaries superior in arms and numbers could not stand their ground, because an invisible power from heaven alone fought with you. He who dared to attack you weighed your armies by mere numbers, yet all his apparatus of war could not withstand the weight of your allies. If you count how often the very air served your interests, the clear skies fought for you, and the heavens poured down rain for you as you wished. Who dared to resist your right hand as you fought with the grace of heaven? How often did your enemies fall by the swords of their own comrades? How often did a man win the victory for you while fighting for the advantage of your foes? For these heavenly gifts, then, make a return by showing compassion to men. Not to spurn the tears of suppliants is the burnt offering of a mystical sacrifice. Consider this above all: what sort of men you have succeeded in the kingdom. If, as is clear, their malice drove them out, their fall must instruct those who follow. The ruin of predecessors teaches those who come after; an earlier fall is always a warning for the future. He does not go to war without an example who looks back at the cause for which his predecessor was cast out. Relying on these things, your Liguria lies prostrate with us and begs you to grant the benefits of your laws to the innocent in such a way that you also absolve the guilty. Mercy counts for little before our God if all it means is that harm does not fall on those who are free of guilt. To forgive faults is heavenly; to punish them is earthly." After this he fell silent.

Then the most eminent king began to speak, and as he spoke, fear gripped hearts anxious to know his will: "Venerable bishop, I look up to you for the light of your merits, and in the time of confusion you laid up many kindnesses with me which you ought to enjoy now that peace has returned. Yet the necessity of ruling, which hems us in, does not everywhere open the way to the mercy you urge, and amid the hard circumstances of a newborn empire the usefulness of severity drives out the sweetness of compassion. My claim rests on the testimony of heavenly examples. We read that a prince gave offense because he saved from death an enemy whom heaven had destined to die. His leniency earned the punishment that strictness could have inflicted. Whoever declines to take vengeance takes it upon himself. Whoever spares his enemy when he has him in his power either weakens or despises the force of divine judgment. Those who have plainly not followed grace must be restrained by justice. Whoever pardons present faults hands vices down to posterity. As for what you say about the patience of our Redeemer, the milk of grace truly embraces those whom the strictness of the law has formed. No sick man has ever been brought by a physician to a full cure except by one who first cut away the rotting limbs with the knife and drew out the filth hidden deep in the bowels. Whoever lets criminals go unpunished urges the innocent to crime. Yet because earthly powers cannot resist your prayers, to which heaven assents, we will pardon the offense of all without exception. No one's head shall fall for his guilt, since you can also prevail with our God to make wicked minds turn from the perversity of their purpose. A few, however, whom I know to have been instigators of evil, I will merely deprive of residence in their own districts, lest some crisis arise and find supporters close at hand, and wars break out again, helped on by the successes of the wicked." Having said this, the most excellent king ordered the illustrious Urbicus to be summoned. He bore all the burdens of the palace and had surpassed Cicero in eloquence and Cato in fairness. The king commanded him to issue a pragmatic decree of general amnesty. Urbicus, always most ready for any act of kindness, at once drew it up with such brevity and clarity that even those kinds of offenses which had been thought to be excepted were understood to be abolished.

Meanwhile the most excellent king ordered the venerable bishop Epiphanius to be summoned privately and addressed him in these words: "Glorious bishop, understand the weight of our judgment from the decision itself: though there are clearly so many bishops within the bounds of our kingdom, you above all are chosen for so great a matter, as if you were the only one. And given your merit, no empty reputation is deceiving those who judge you so. You alone are rightly thought to be such a man, by whose splendor the light of lesser stars is dimmed, as by the orb of the moon, and the rays of feeble lights are darkened by the brilliant light of your conscience. Who would look for a night lamp where the radiance of the sun is blazing? Who would need the help of a candle where the pyre of faith is kindled in ever-burning furnaces? Finally, I must send the kind of man whom the one who receives him will gladly listen to. You see that every region of Italy has been robbed of its native farmers. To my sorrow the field once rich in crops brings forth thorns and growths no one planted, and Liguria, that mother of the human harvest, which used to have a numerous progeny of farmers, now bereaved and barren, shows a hungry sod to our eyes. The land appeals to me: wherever I look, it grieves me with a face rich in vineyards but untouched by the plough. O grief! No drink touches the lips of those whom antiquity named Oenotrians for their abundance of wine. Though it was the cruel Burgundian who did these things, we have allowed them if we do not set them right. Are we failing to help our ravaged homeland while gold lies stored away in our keeping? What does it matter whether we bend the minds of our adversaries with money or with the sword? To have offered the enemy what wins minds is to have conquered; to have hidden it away is to be defeated. Take up, then, with Christ's help, the burden of this task, from which we may share a common reward in the promise of heaven, for this new title of praise is added to your own distinctions: to triumph through your hands over those who attacked us, without bloodshed. Their prince is Gundobad, in whom long acquaintance has planted reverence for you, and who is spurred by a great longing to see you. Believe me, the sight of you will be the ransom for Italy's captives. I will consider the people I long for as good as redeemed if such a redeemer comes to those lands. How powerfully will the eyes to which we offer you be won over! But why do I hold back the hands for which the fields are calling? I promise you that the state of Liguria will revive. I promise the joy of the soil, and fertility returning after the exile beyond the Alps. The gold lent to you is only an accessory to the cause you will plead as so great an envoy."

To this Epiphanius, the light of bishops, replied: "Venerable prince, if words could encompass the joy with which you have filled my heart, I would pour out a continuous stream of unrehearsed speech in return for the riches of your merits. But the tears of joy show how far my speech is cut short and denied success. Exultation now brings forth tears, though they are the offspring of sorrow. Understand, then, that in giving thanks to the best of kings, both on our behalf and on his own, I can feel more than I can say. Shall I first recall that you have surpassed all the emperors before you in justice, or in the practice of war, or in piety, which is more excellent than these? You have grounds to accuse the former rulers of our people: you ransom those whom they very often either allowed to be made captives or made captive themselves. We read that David, as an example of singular praise, attained nearness to heaven chiefly because he spared his enemy Saul when Saul was delivered into his hands, and as a testimony of the power granted him cut off a piece of his garment, by which he proved both his opportunity and his intention. Good God! With what great reward will you receive the deed of this man, who is negotiating for the freedom of so many thousands of the oppressed, you who exalted David for sparing the blood of a single man! Carry through, then, with all speed, what you have begun. Gladly bring the offering of your good fortune, and spur me on, though I am ready, so that you are not held back by the obstacle of delay in offering so fragrant a sacrifice. It will be for Christ our Redeemer to grant, as we infer from the works that it will happen, that you may truly offer your burnt offerings by my hands. I ask, however, that by the indulgence of your clemency Victor, bishop of the city of Turin, be joined to me as companion and partner on this journey, for it is clear that the sum of all virtues is found in him. With him as my companion, I promise with confidence in our God that no result will be denied to our petitions."

When he heard this, the most eminent king gave his assent, and the awe-inspiring bishop said farewell and departed. At once funds to be carried for the ransom were assigned and received. He set out and came tirelessly to Pavia. It was still March, sluggish with winter, which laid icy bridles on the rivers, and the ridges of the Alps, white with snow, threatened death to those who would cross them; yet the ardor of faith overcame the deadly cold and the clods frozen hard. He whose foundation the rock has made firm never slips on the ice. So, having arranged the provisions for his journey, he set out. You would have said that he was driving on everything that necessity might have held back. He would not endure delay even to take food, and though that path full of dangers alarmed every one of those with him, he alone, amid the perils, did not know how to fear, for the sure hope of life went with him. Meanwhile fame, which always went before his journeys and diligently prepared the way, went ahead and so filled the Gauls with reports of his distinctions that they were stirred as if by the coming or presence of a heavenly power. People of every age and sex ran together, and those whom long distances separated from the road were brought near by their eagerness. Whatever each had of value he offered, and if he did not have it, he bought it elsewhere: everywhere was a homeland, everywhere lavish generosity. The travelers' tables were heaped with fare they had not bought, and strangers enjoyed without paying the foods that the inhabitants themselves could have only by buying them. Then he distributed what had been given to whatever needy people he found. In his lodging and out of it he fed the wretched, and nothing brought to him could be withheld from the use of the poor.

In this way, with wonderful speed, he entered Lyon, where Rusticius then held the episcopal see. Even when his secular rank only foreshadowed his future office, this man always showed himself a priest, and under the guise of public life he acted as a governor of the church. Filled with an abundance of spiritual joy, he crossed the river Rhône to meet Epiphanius on his arrival, asked the reason for his journey, and informed him of the king's cunning ways. So that clever objections or replies should not catch him unprepared, Epiphanius fortified himself within the inner chamber of his heart by rehearsing the contest beforehand. When Gundobad, lord of that land, learned that he had come, he said to his men: "Go and see the man whom I have always likened, both in merits and in face, to the person of Lawrence the martyr. Ask when he wishes to see us, and when he gives the word, invite him." Soon the whole throng of Christians attending the prince flocked to him, and they were seized with boundless admiration, because his fame, spread by so many tongues and great though it was, proved so much less than the man himself. In its poverty of words it could never do him justice, though in other cases it was richer than it ought to be. So a day was fixed for him to see the king. When he entered, he greeted him, and each rejoiced at the sight of the other. Epiphanius gave the eminent Victor leave to open the embassy, if he himself wished [?]; but Victor, being always most ready for every humility, referred the whole weight of it back to him.

At once our bishop, the glory of Italy, began to address the king in these words: "Most esteemed prince, an inexpressible love for you has for some time laid upon me the task of making war on this journey against nature and season, and of not fearing the dangers of the ice-crusted mountain, which, once it has bound its waters into metal, threatens a death congealed out of liquid. I have crossed snowy passes in months not meant for them; I have set my steps where in their proper season the force of the cold would have held them fast. In short, I did not fear death, so that I might swiftly bring you the reward of eternal light. I am called to bear witness in heaven between two excellent kings, if you graciously grant what he mercifully asks. Divide the gift of the Lord's promise in an even balance, and when both of you have more, no one will mourn a loss. Contend, most invincible leaders, and outdo one another in carrying out the mystic precepts. In this contest the victor will take the prize in such a way that the vanquished does not lose his reward. Follow my counsel, and you will both stand superior, both equal. He wishes to ransom the captives: you, without price, return them to their native soil. Believe me, in this cause no one will receive more richly, no one more greatly, than the one who receives nothing. His side will be cheated of its reward, and the other's gain will pass to your profit, if you resolve to give away those whom it would be glorious even to sell. Oh, what a loss of the divine promise the gold offered in this business inflicts on the one offering it, if it is sent back! Or what poverty it brings, if it is accepted! Money despised will make your armies rich; money acquired will make them beggars. Hear the voices of the suppliant Italians and calmly admit the prayers of those who rely on you. Hear Italy, never estranged from you and trusting much in the clemency of your heart. If she could speak with one voice, she would say this: 'How often, if you remember, did you set your iron-clad breast against the enemy for me? How often did you fight with counsel, so that wars would not take me by surprise, so that none of mine would be led captive to any part of the world? Those whom you now hold, you nurtured. Your valor did me a treacherous kindness, if the guardian has seized those whom it protected from outsiders. Who, bound in the knots of chains, would not shed more abundant tears at his harsh lot, when his liberator was driving him into servitude? Who would slip away when he heard the clash of your arms, in which, in their need, they had found the safest refuge? A noble matron, her hands crushed against her neck as she was dragged off to chains, promised herself that you would be her avenger. A virgin, facing the ravisher's snares, believed that her chastity, if lost, would displease you. In sum, those were captured whom no one found fleeing. The toiling stock of farmers, offspring trained to the hard mattock, whom an unschooled simplicity feeds on their own land, cried nothing else in their own defense when their necks were bound with thongs and tight bonds tied their hands: "We know and plainly recognize you—are you not our Burgundians? Take care lest you have to excuse what you are doing before the pious king, and try to hide these crimes behind the customs of civilized men. How often have these hands which you presume to bind paid tribute to our common lord? We know that he did not order these things to be done." The wretched took comfort in this authority. Yet trust in your integrity caused many to be killed, because as captives they answered too proudly.' Restore, then, the survivors to their homeland, restore them to their origin, restore them to your own glory. The former lord loves the province which the present one also embraces. Send them back, though it be to another's rule, men who will know that even there they are yours. For we owe little gratitude to the rule of one to whose mercy we owe nothing. Clear of briars that Liguria you know so well, and fill it with cultivation. She will understand how much she is indebted to your gifts if she ever recognizes her own face again. It has always been your nature to indulge suppliants, just as to crush the proud. So, most mighty in both, you will win triumphs there by the sword, here by moderation. Be moved by our tears and the tears of our people. So may a lawful heir grow up for you in the succession to this kingdom, and through the hope of grown offspring may you live again in the government of the Burgundians. And though you grant this to God, add this too: that you are not bestowing it on strangers. Already the lord of Italy is joined to you by the tie of kinship. Let the release of the captives be a Latin largesse for your son's bride; let him offer his betrothed a gift that Christ also may accept." When he had said this, he signaled to his holy colleague Victor and rose, and weeping, together with all who stood nearby, they bowed their heads down to the king's breast.

Then the most esteemed king, a man rich in speech, wealthy in the resources of eloquence and a fluent advocate, answered words with words: "As a champion of peace you know nothing of the laws of war, and as an author of concord you tear apart the terms settled by the sword. What you consider an error is the law of combatants; enmities know nothing of the bridle which you, radiance of Christian light, hold out. No one joins to battle the moderation that is extolled by the brilliance of your speech, excellent guide. It is the rule of those who fight that whatever is unlawful then becomes lawful. Peace, perhaps, may claim for itself the things you have recounted; but whoever has not harmed his enemy has helped him. Little by little an adversary is cut away from the mass of his kingdom when the roots of his rule are severed by force. I paid back to the king of those parts the insult which you think I inflicted. Mocked by the semblance of a treaty, I strove for nothing more eagerly than to recognize open enemies, as caution requires. Yet may God grant his assent, so that the treaty now made firm between us may be kept for a long age: that side will find constant in friendship the man they felt to be ruinous to them while he was at strife. You, however, holy men, return untroubled to the houses where you are staying, while I weigh what serves my soul and my kingdom and then declare what it befits me to grant." Having heard this, the bishops withdrew.

Then he summoned Laconius. The king has always safely entrusted to him confidence in both affairs and words. The privilege of his birth and the curule chairs of his ancestors have raised him high through the marks of a masterly integrity, and the king confers with him whenever he is considering anything pious or religious. And since his nobility is not allied with vices, nor is the light of his nature bound to allurements, whenever the king wishes to do some kindness, this man, when called in, urges him to double it. The prince said to him: "Go, Laconius, and spread all the sails of your shorthand. Both the bishop and the blessed Epiphanius have been gladly heard by us, and your tears, which reveal the mind, testified that you were moved by his entreaties when he was speaking before us. Go, and with a full heart dictate decrees by which you may break the bonds of that harshest compact, at once and for all the Italians: whoever were made captives of our Burgundians through fear of captivity, whoever were brought here by the necessity of hunger or the fear of danger, and finally whoever were ceded or handed over by the consent of their own prince—let our decree set them free. But for the few whom our men seized from the dominion of their adversaries in the heat of battle, as it were, let them receive some small price, lest the fortunes of war become hateful to them if, having endured its dangers, they get none of its gains."

Following the venerable king's command, that tireless man set out the forms and particulars of the pardon in nimble words and brought the documents to the distinguished bishop. Epiphanius received them with the devotion of one who had long awaited them and warmly embraced the bearer of so great a gift. Once the news became known, so great a throng of this now-free multitude suddenly appeared that you would have thought the countryside of Gaul emptied even of its inhabitants. For I am a witness of this: it was through my hands that the bishop's order issued passes for the frontier gates, and four hundred people were released in a single day from the city of Lyon alone to return to Italy. We learned beyond doubt that the same was done in the various cities of Savoy and of other provinces, so that, of those freed by the prayers of the most blessed man alone, more than six thousand souls were restored to their native lands. Of those who were ransomed with gold I could not learn the exact number, because many among them also escaped by flight. So it came about that the opportunity to cross over, granted at that time, sufficed for the liberation of all who had been subjugated. After that heap of money had been spent, however, Syagria, who is the treasury of the church there, at once supplied what was needed for the expenses of the ransom. Her life calls for a lengthy narrative; it is enough, though, that she be recognized by her works, which surpass words. Avitus, bishop of Vienne, the most eminent man among the Gauls, also gave, in whom learning has lodged itself as in the inn of a shining house. Why say more?
