It was by their gold, for the most part, that the youth of Liguria was not led any longer into servitude to the Gauls. The eminent man stayed in one place in that region [?], lest the ferocity of their masters hinder those living far away. He was at Geneva, where Godigisel, the king's brother, had established his home; following the pattern of his brother's decision, Godigisel made himself a partner in his good works. In a short time such great phalanxes of the freed were sent back that you could see the roads far and wide teeming with columns of people returning, praising our God and also the most splendid bishop Epiphanius, by whose ministry and toil they had been rescued. And so that our light should not be deprived of the trophy of so great a gift, nor that most beautiful spectacle be taken from his eyes, he himself returned with them. You could see a free people led in heavenly triumph, and the ground wet not with the blood of sacrificial victims but with the tears of the rejoicing, while the leader of these cohorts mounted the chariot of Elijah and was swept heavenward in a four-horsed course, as his merit deserved. Not so did Alexander, the Pellaean prince, whom empty praise called the pacifier of the world, lead off a swarm of captured nations as this man brought them back. See, then we learned that the minds of armed men were overcome by holiness, and that a prince who had always set his breast against lances yielded to the prayers of the chosen one. Learn from this, reader, how much sharper the blade of words was than the blade of iron: speech conquered one from whom swords had shrunk back. So, while the bishop was returning to Pavia in the third month with such a trophy, he came to Tarantaise (for so a town near the Alps is called), and there a certain woman was suffering severe torment from an unclean spirit; as soon as she received his blessing, she went away freed. He himself appeared before his own people unexpectedly, before eyes that did not look for him. He was suddenly seen, he of whom scarcely anyone believed any news could be heard.

But as soon as he had returned, he wearied his mind with cares, as was his custom, lest those to whom our God had granted release through him should be troubled about possessing their own property. He was concerned above all for persons of noble birth, for whom a harsher calamity might await among their own people if they came home only to endure a life of want and, after the hardships of exile, lost the sole consolation that mercy had left them. He did not wish to go in person to the most invincible King Theoderic at once, lest by being present he should seem to demand a return for his labor in thanks or in gifts; for whoever, having carried out the commands of princes, announces in person what he has done, is demanding a reward as if it were owed. This, then, that man of the keenest insight foresaw and was eager to avoid. Yet he wrote, and entrusted to letters the account of what had been done, so as not to be judged contemptuous for keeping silent or immoderate and arrogant for presenting himself. How much more, admirable bishop, did your absence then achieve, how much did your humility, once perceived, command! Let those say it whom you made exceedingly rich out of exiles. So everything that the singular bishop asked in writing from the most pious king on behalf of the wretched he obtained without delay. The king calmly granted the petitioner all he wished, believing that the bishop would count as sufficient recompense for his labor whatever benefit the ransomed and the poor received through him.

After all who had been recalled were restored to their rights by the indulgence of the incomparable prince, the admirable bishop thought the mass of his troubles was over. But before two years had passed, he was driven from the bosom of the rest he had resolved upon, like a skiff driven out of harbor by another storm. For a burden of taxes scarcely to be borne was being laid on the weak and tottering shoulders of the Ligurians. Again they run to you, comforter of the afflicted. You would teach that it was vain to have restored citizens to their homeland if you did not stand by them when they were endangered on their ancestral soil. And because no one who asked anything of you ever grew weary, you took up the cause of the unfortunate and at once prepared yourself for renewed burdens. You hasten to Ravenna to petition the king for us, the very city you had avoided so that no one there would praise you after your Gallic triumphs. You overcome the threats of the sky and the dangers of storms as if still in the fullness of your years or fortified by bodily strength. Your limbs, however weak, never withdrew from the service of your spirit: cold, rain, the Po, fasting, sailing, danger, thunder, lodging without a roof on the riverbanks, uncertain harbors with scarcely any land, were sweet to your virtue and welcome for the sake of success. Even that most eminent king, who eagerly wished to see you, was saddened by your coming. Your arrival set forth our needs before you spoke, and the dangers you had overcome showed what tears of those who lived with you had driven you on.

When he came before the prince, he began to speak as follows: "Venerable king, hear the prayers of your servants with your accustomed tranquillity of mind. Custom has taught me to ask for what is needed and you to grant it. It is your law, unconquered leader, to show mercy at all times. You have always nourished the hope of future petitions by not refusing present ones, and our confidence in favours once obtained has always opened the way for our pleas to ask you for more. Bestow on your Ligurians what you may later draw from them; grant what you may store up. Indulgence for a season is profit for the time to come. It is the way of a good prince to love fame together with virtue, and to order his kingdom as though it were to pass to the descendants of his line. Insecure lords love only what they receive; the most secure love rather what they remit. So we commit small seeds to the earth so that we may reap them multiplied; the interest is tripled without any wrong done. The wealth of the landholder belongs to the good emperor. Grant Liguria freedom from tax for the present year, you who brought back from foreign lands those who now petition you. How abundant a harvest we have had this year, let your clemency ask those standing here. No one lies to a man whose servants could prove him wrong." To this the prince replied: "Although the weight of enormous expenses presses on us [?], and we are constantly giving gifts to envoys for the sake of these very people's peace, yet the force of your merits reverently intervenes in our deliberations. Whatever you enjoin must be done; everything you command pleases us. For we reckon that whatever you yourself take away from us is added to our gains. Nothing you ask for is asked as if by chance, since you have many claims on us that you could call in. Nevertheless, we will remit two parts of the fiscal assessment for the present indiction and collect only a third, so that neither the straitness of our treasury brings greater losses on the Romans nor your petition fails to bring back the joy your homeland is awaiting." In this way the supreme bishop gave thanks to the king, and bidding him farewell, he departed. Alas for grief and groaning! He hastened tirelessly to everyone, as if with the zeal of a final duty or a last visit. And though his own house poured out crowds of the Christian multitude, he himself went into the inner rooms of everyone. No one, dulled by the coarseness of the human mind, was touched by so grim a suspicion as that his departure was at hand, though he himself foresaw it by the revelation of the Spirit. In snowy weather, the kind that usually drives people to take shelter, he left Ravenna and came swiftly through all the cities of Emilia, as though hurrying to the shelter of the tomb. To all the priests along the way he was generous, sociable and affable, and, as if leaving behind a legacy, he surpassed even himself. But as soon as he entered Parma, a city on that same road, a humour congealed in his vitals, which doctors call catarrh, flooded through him; penetrating to the marrow, it was then raging to the ruin of the whole people. But why are you afraid, my speech? Why do you dread the rocks of shipwreck like a sailor? Willing or not, you must tell of the death of one whose life has been told, however briefly, since no lengthening of this little book, no drawing out of the praise set forth, can conceal his passing. And though the ship under sail may flee from Scylla's dogs and the gaping jaws of Charybdis, which threaten danger with their crashing roar, the shipwreck of his death cannot be avoided. Why do I fear to tell of the weeping that ceaseless outpouring of tears must always show? So, as he drew near the town of Pavia, now so wretched, he seemed cheerful and well. But although he entered amid everyone's rejoicing at his return, he at once turned their joy to tears, letting it be known that he was ill that very day, and more gravely ill the next. And as the sickness grew greater day by day, the doctors' lack of skill only aided it. The people stood about, murmuring and stunned, seeing in one man the fall of the whole province and fearing the funeral of the world. On the seventh day came the unexpected crime, the unspeakable calamity, the inexpressible grief. But when the most blessed bishop saw that, having cast off the burden of the flesh, he would soon fly up to the pure brightness of heaven—he whose saying had always been "For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain"—with glad heart and serene face he repeated again and again those little verses of David: "I will sing of your mercies, O Lord, forever; from generation to generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth," and also: "Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit." Secure in his perfection, he added as well: "My heart is strengthened in the Lord, and my horn is exalted in God my salvation," so that his heavenly soul, resounding with hymns and songs even in death, might return to its home. It brought him to the tomb in the fifty-eighth year of his age, thirty of which he had spent in this priestly way of life, which you, reader, see sketched here, though only in extracts.

For I must not pass over in silence that his holy remains, up to the third day, when they were laid to rest with the greatest veneration, appeared to the eyes of all clothed in such light and beauty that the face of the dead man bore the mark of the splendour of his life, and that glorious vessel, in which the treasure of the great King had truly been enclosed, was believed to have already received the glory stored up for it. What rivers of tears there were, how much lamentation, I will pass over in silence, lest after the passing of so many years I as a writer should stir up fresh grief. Every mother who came there cried out that her son had been set free by him; every wife, her husband; every sister, her brother; every unmarried man, himself. In short, in that vast multitude and gathering of what I would boldly call the whole world, there was no one who did not owe something to his kindnesses.

But now, I beg you, let us refrain from mourning; let us smooth the brow that sorrow has furrowed. The one whose death we grieve on earth possesses the heights with God. But what am I to do, when sobs break up the words of your consoler, tears flood my face, and everything I say echoes with a moan? I know too that a weeping consoler never does well coming to one who weeps. I have spent these words on our holy father and most learned teacher, fitted for the task by affection rather than by knowledge, gathering a few little flowers from his way of life, as is the custom of those on a long journey, who do not greet everyone they meet. You, soul mighty in the presence of our Redeemer, grant me that, free of care and unburdened in heart, I may pay you, in purity, the pure praises that are your due. For the rest, do not abandon one who, after God, places his trust in you, and make him whom you honoured with the titles of religion a sharer with the religious in the divine promise.
